cards.title: Compassionate Mental Health Care
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 8 · Level 3

cards.title: Welcome to Level 3
cards.body: At the highest level of the GNPS pathway, Global Nursing Professionals move beyond individual care. You will lead recovery-oriented services, reduce restrictive practice, mentor teams and advocate for equity on a global scale.

bullets.label: This level builds advanced capability across
bullets.text: This level builds advanced capability across leadership, trauma-informed systems, digital mental health and workforce wellbeing.

bullets.label: Lead rights-based, recovery-oriented mental health services
Strengthen suicide, violence and restrictive-practice prevention
Design, evaluate and sustain service-improvement initiatives
Use digital technologies safely and contribute to global mental health equity

cards.title: Why This Learning Matters
cards.body: Mental health harm frequently arises from fragmented care, stigma, coercive systems and failure to recognise physical illness alongside mental health needs.

bullets.label: Global Nursing Professionals identify these
bullets.text: Global Nursing Professionals identify these systemic connections and lead practical improvements that protect dignity, safety and recovery for every person in their care.

cards.title: Your Learning Goal
cards.body: Lead. Improve. Advocate.

bullets.label: By completing Level 3, you will be equipped to
bullets.text: By completing Level 3, you will be equipped to lead mental health quality and safety initiatives, use evidence and data to strengthen services, support colleagues and contribute to recovery-oriented care — locally and globally.

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Leading Recovery-Oriented & Rights-Based Services

bullets.label: Leadership in mental health means creating
bullets.text: Leadership in mental health means creating services where people are treated with dignity, hope and genuine partnership. Global Nursing Professionals model recovery-oriented practice and ensure organisational systems support — not undermine — these values.

cards.title: Core Concepts: Recovery Leadership
cards.body: Recovery Leadership

bullets.label: Care planning, language and routines must
bullets.text: Care planning, language and routines must reflect personal goals, strengths and informed choice — not clinical convenience.

bullets.label: People with lived experience participate as
bullets.text: People with lived experience participate as genuine partners in service design, education and evaluation — not symbolic representatives.

bullets.label: Reflective supervision, debriefing and psychological safety help staff manage complexity while sustaining compassion.
Leaders challenge discrimination, promote
bullets.text: Leaders challenge discrimination, promote supported decision-making and ensure mental illness never reduces access to physical healthcare.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Recovery-Oriented Care Planning
cards.body: The Challenge

bullets.label: A service reviews its care plans with people
bullets.text: A service reviews its care plans with people who use the service and discovers that goals are written mainly by clinicians, with little meaningful patient input.

bullets.label: The team redesigns planning around each
bullets.text: The team redesigns planning around each person's own recovery goals and begins measuring participation at every review meeting.

bullets.label: Outcome: Greater ownership, improved engagement and plans that truly reflect what matters to the person.

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Reducing Restrictive Practice & Strengthening Safety Systems

bullets.label: Restrictive practices can cause significant
bullets.text: Restrictive practices can cause significant physical and psychological harm. Global Nursing Professionals analyse why restriction occurs and lead safer, trauma-informed alternatives — while maintaining protection from serious risk.

cards.title: Core Concepts: Safety Systems
cards.body: Restrictive-Practice Review

bullets.label: Seclusion, restraint and forced treatment must
bullets.text: Seclusion, restraint and forced treatment must be monitored by frequency, population and context. Every event should prompt learning.

bullets.label: Services should maximise safety, choice, collaboration and predictability — avoiding practices that recreate trauma.
Reliable assessment, safety planning, post-crisis follow-up and communication across transitions all reduce risk.
Staffing, ward design, sensory environments and access to meaningful activity all influence behavioural escalation.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Reducing Restraint on Evening Shifts
cards.body: Measure

bullets.label: A unit with high evening-shift restraint use
bullets.text: A unit with high evening-shift restraint use underwent systematic review. By addressing environmental and staffing root causes rather than individual behaviour, the service reduced restrictive practice and improved safety for all.

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Quality Improvement, Integrated Care & Population Mental Health

bullets.label: Mental health outcomes are shaped by service
bullets.text: Mental health outcomes are shaped by service quality, physical health, housing, social connection and access to care. Improvement requires collaboration across traditional service boundaries.

cards.title: Quality Improvement: Core Concepts
cards.body: Why It Matters

bullets.label: Reliable data reveals where care falls short.
bullets.text: Reliable data reveals where care falls short. By measuring across outcome, process, experience and equity, nursing leaders can target improvement where it creates the greatest benefit.

bullets.label: Connecting mental and physical healthcare
bullets.text: Connecting mental and physical healthcare pathways remains one of the most critical — and most overlooked — opportunities for improving outcomes.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Metabolic Monitoring Improvement
cards.body: The Problem

bullets.label: A community service identifies poor metabolic
bullets.text: A community service identifies poor metabolic monitoring for people receiving antipsychotic medications — a significant but preventable physical health risk.

bullets.label: Clinical reminders and primary-care communication established
Peer-supported education for service users implemented
Completion rates and follow-up consistency
bullets.text: Completion rates and follow-up consistency improved significantly, reducing cardiovascular risk in a vulnerable population.

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Digital Mental Health & Global Collaboration

bullets.label: Digital platforms, telehealth, apps and
bullets.text: Digital platforms, telehealth, apps and predictive tools can expand mental health support — but they also create risks involving privacy, exclusion, misinformation and over-reliance on algorithms. Global professionals use technology critically and ethically.

cards.title: Digital Mental Health: Key Principles
cards.body: Tele-Mental Health

bullets.label: Virtual care improves access but requires
bullets.text: Virtual care improves access but requires identity confirmation, privacy safeguards, emergency plans and awareness of assessment limitations.

bullets.label: Digital tools must be evidence-informed and
bullets.text: Digital tools must be evidence-informed and transparent. They support — but must never replace — urgent clinical assessment.

bullets.label: Predictive tools may reflect biased data.
bullets.text: Predictive tools may reflect biased data. Nurses must retain professional judgement and clearly explain algorithmic limitations to teams.

bullets.label: Adapt global learning to local culture and
bullets.text: Adapt global learning to local culture and resources. Support accessible, culturally relevant and sustainable care models worldwide.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Rural Telehealth Implementation
cards.body: The Challenge

bullets.label: A rural service needed to extend mental health review access to people who could not travel to clinic settings.
Privacy guidance and consent protocols established
Telephone alternatives available for people without internet access
Technology improved access without becoming the only route to care — maintaining equity and safety.

cards.title: The GNPS Learning Pathway
cards.body: Level 1 — Qualified Nurse

bullets.label: Foundations in recovery, communication, assessment, common conditions and safety
Complex risk, medication, law and culturally safe international practice
Rights-based services, quality improvement, integrated care and global mental health innovation

cards.title: Program 8 Complete — Well Done
cards.body: By completing GNPS Program 8 · Level 3, you have developed the advanced perspective of a Global Nursing Professional — prepared to lead recovery-oriented services, reduce restrictive practice, improve systems and advocate for equitable mental wellbeing worldwide.

cards.title: Leading Recovery-Oriented & Rights-Based Services
cards.body: Leadership in mental health means creating services where people are treated with dignity, hope and partnership. Global Nursing Professionals model recovery-oriented practice and ensure organisational systems support — rather than undermine — these values.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Champion recovery-oriented mental health care across your service
Foster meaningful service-user and family involvement
Enable reflective practice and staff wellbeing
Drive anti-stigma action and rights-based care

cards.title: Recovery Leadership
cards.body: What Does Recovery Leadership Look Like?

bullets.label: Leaders ensure that care planning, language,
bullets.text: Leaders ensure that care planning, language, routines and evaluation all reflect the personal goals, strengths and choices of those receiving care — not just clinical priorities.

bullets.label: Person-centred goal setting in every care plan
Regular evaluation of patient outcomes and satisfaction
Routine structures designed around individual needs

cards.title: Co-Production in Mental Health Services
cards.body: People with lived experience must participate in service design, education and evaluation as genuine partners — not as symbolic representatives or token voices.

bullets.label: Co-production is not consultation. It is shared decision-making power at every level of the service.

cards.title: Workforce Culture & Psychological Safety
cards.body: Reflective Supervision

bullets.label: Regular structured supervision supports staff to process complex emotional experiences and maintain compassionate care
After critical incidents, structured debriefs help teams learn, recover and prevent burnout
Staff must feel safe to raise concerns, admit mistakes and seek support without fear of blame

cards.title: Rights, Anti-Stigma & Equitable Access
cards.body: Why This Matters

bullets.label: People living with mental illness are at
bullets.text: People living with mental illness are at significantly higher risk of preventable physical health conditions, yet often receive less thorough physical assessments.

bullets.label: Leaders must actively challenge the systemic
bullets.text: Leaders must actively challenge the systemic biases that reduce access to full healthcare — within their own teams and across the wider organisation.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Redesigning Care Planning
cards.body: Review

bullets.label: When a service reviewed its care plans with
bullets.text: When a service reviewed its care plans with people who use the service, it discovered that goals were written primarily by clinicians. By redesigning the process around personal recovery goals and measuring participation at review meetings, the team achieved a measurable shift towards genuine co-production.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Align Systems with Recovery Values

bullets.label: Ensure every organisational process — from care planning to staff appraisal — reflects recovery principles
Move beyond tokenism to genuine partnership in decision-making, design and evaluation
A psychologically safe workforce delivers better, more compassionate care
Advocate for equitable treatment within your team and across the wider healthcare system

cards.title: Ready to Lead with Compassion
cards.body: "Support recovery. Promote wellbeing."

bullets.label: As a Global Nursing Professional, you are
bullets.text: As a Global Nursing Professional, you are equipped to lead services that uphold dignity, rights and hope — empowering both the people you care for and the teams you lead.

cards.title: Section 2 Overview
cards.body: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems

bullets.label: Restrictive practices — including seclusion,
bullets.text: Restrictive practices — including seclusion, restraint, and forced treatment — can cause lasting physical and psychological harm. Global Nursing Professionals are expected to analyse why restriction occurs and lead safer, trauma-informed alternatives without compromising protection from serious risk.

bullets.label: Review incidents to identify patterns and drivers.
Use trauma-informed practices to reduce restraints.
Enhance policies and training to sustain safety.
This section equips nurses to move beyond reactive responses and build systems that prevent escalation before it begins.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Examine frequency, duration, and population patterns to identify inequity and system failure.
Design care environments that maximise safety, choice, and predictability for all patients.
Build reliable suicide and violence prevention pathways across care transitions.
Measure whether evidence-based alternatives genuinely reduce harm and improve outcomes.

cards.title: Core Concept 1: Restrictive-Practice Review
cards.body: Seclusion, restraint, and forced treatment must be systematically monitored across four dimensions:

bullets.label: Every restrictive event should trigger a structured review and a learning response — not just documentation.

cards.title: Core Concept 2: Trauma-Informed Systems
cards.body: What Is Trauma-Informed Care?

bullets.label: A trauma-informed service recognises that many
bullets.text: A trauma-informed service recognises that many patients have histories of harm and that restrictive practices can recreate traumatic experiences. Systems must be redesigned around four principles:

bullets.label: Physical and emotional safety for patients and staff
Offering meaningful options at every stage of care
Shared decision-making with patients and families
Consistent, transparent routines that reduce anxiety

cards.title: Core Concept 3: Suicide Prevention Systems
cards.body: Effective suicide prevention is a system, not a single assessment. Reliable pathways reduce risk across every transition point in care.

bullets.label: Structured, validated tools used consistently across the team
Co-produced plans that are personalised, accessible, and reviewed regularly
Proactive contact within 24–72 hours after crisis episodes
Clear handover information shared across all care settings

cards.title: Core Concept 4: Workplace and Environmental Safety
cards.body: The Environment as a Clinical Tool

bullets.label: Behavioural escalation is rarely random. Ward
bullets.text: Behavioural escalation is rarely random. Ward conditions directly shape patient response. Nursing professionals must assess and advocate for environmental changes as part of clinical practice.

bullets.label: Crowding and noise elevate distress and aggression
Understaffing increases response delays and risk
Sensory rooms reduce the need for physical intervention
Structured activity provides purpose and reduces boredom-driven escalation

cards.title: Clinical Example: Reducing Evening Restraint
cards.body: A unit identifies high restraint use during evening shifts. A structured review reveals multiple contributing system factors — not individual patient behaviour.

bullets.label: Crowding, limited evening activity,
bullets.text: Crowding, limited evening activity, inconsistent staffing, and delayed medication reviews all coincide with peak restraint incidents.

bullets.label: Sensory support tools, a revised staffing
bullets.text: Sensory support tools, a revised staffing pattern, environmental redesign, and faster medication review pathways are implemented.

bullets.label: Restraint frequency, duration, and staff
bullets.text: Restraint frequency, duration, and staff incident rates are tracked over time to confirm whether change has reduced harm.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Look Beyond the Individual

bullets.label: Restrictive events are rarely caused by one
bullets.text: Restrictive events are rarely caused by one patient. Examine the system conditions — staffing, environment, routine — that create the risk.

bullets.label: Identify patterns and inequity through regular review of restrictive-practice data. Who is most affected, and when?
Intervene early with de-escalation, sensory tools, and meaningful engagement — before a situation becomes a crisis.
Evaluate whether alternatives genuinely reduce
bullets.text: Evaluate whether alternatives genuinely reduce harm. Intention is not enough — evidence of outcome is essential for continuous improvement.

cards.title: Section 2 Complete
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series · Programme 8 · Mental Health Nursing

bullets.text: You have now completed Section 2. Apply the principles of trauma-informed systems thinking and restrictive-practice review in your clinical reflections and NCLEX preparation.

bullets.label: Proceed to Section 3 to continue building your Global Nursing Professional competencies.
Consider a clinical situation where system
bullets.text: Consider a clinical situation where system factors — not patient behaviour — drove an escalation. What could have changed?

cards.title: Mental Health Nursing: Quality Improvement, Integrated Care & Population Mental Health
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 8 · Level 3

cards.title: Why This Section Matters
cards.body: Mental health outcomes are not determined by clinical care alone. Housing, social connection, trauma history, physical health, and access to services all shape recovery. Meaningful improvement demands collaboration across traditional service boundaries — placing the person at the centre of every decision.

bullets.label: "Support recovery. Promote wellbeing." — GNPS Programme 8 Core Principle

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Apply mental health data to identify and prioritise service improvement opportunities.
Apply structured quality-improvement methods to clinical practice settings.
Promote coordinated physical and mental healthcare across service boundaries.
Address social determinants and identify unequal access or outcomes across populations.

cards.title: Quality Improvement Priorities in Mental Health
cards.body: Quality priorities guide where improvement efforts should be focused. Common areas in mental health nursing include:

bullets.label: Ensuring timely contact after discharge or crisis episodes.
Tracking metabolic, cardiac, and general health in mental health patients.
Reducing prescribing errors and improving adherence monitoring.
Minimising avoidable readmissions through planned transitions of care.

cards.title: Integrated Care: Coordinating Across Services
cards.body: People with mental health needs often require support from multiple services simultaneously. Integrated care means organising these services around the person, not in professional silos.

bullets.label: Community, inpatient, and crisis teams delivering specialist psychiatric care.
GPs and practice nurses managing physical conditions alongside mental health needs.
A&E and crisis response teams supporting acute mental health presentations.
Dual-diagnosis support addressing co-occurring addiction and mental illness.
Housing, welfare, and social support addressing the wider determinants of health.

cards.title: Measuring What Matters
cards.body: Effective quality improvement depends on selecting the right measures. A balanced set of metrics reveals whether change is truly working — or simply shifting a problem elsewhere.

bullets.label: Did the team follow the agreed pathway?
Did service users feel heard and respected?
Did improvement in one area create problems elsewhere?

cards.title: Equity: Who Benefits? Who Is Left Behind?
cards.body: Improvement data must be disaggregated to expose hidden inequalities. A service that appears to perform well on average may still be failing specific groups.

bullets.label: Examine disparities in diagnosis, detention rates, and access.
Identify whether young people, older adults, or gender minorities are underserved.
Rural and remote communities often face longer waits and fewer specialists.
Poverty, unemployment and housing instability compound mental health risk.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Metabolic Monitoring in Practice
cards.body: The Problem

bullets.label: A community mental health service identified
bullets.text: A community mental health service identified poor metabolic monitoring for patients receiving antipsychotic medications — a known but often overlooked risk.

bullets.label: Shared physical health pathway introduced across teams
Automated clinical reminders for monitoring checks
Structured communication with primary care practitioners
Peer-supported education for service users on physical health
Completion rates for monitoring improved
bullets.text: Completion rates for monitoring improved significantly. Follow-up rates increased and cross-service communication strengthened.

cards.title: The Quality Improvement Cycle
cards.body: Define Problem

bullets.label: Each phase builds on the last. Sustainable
bullets.text: Each phase builds on the last. Sustainable improvement requires ongoing measurement, honest evaluation, and a commitment to including those most often overlooked.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Define the problem with reliable data

bullets.label: Assumptions are not enough — evidence must drive every improvement priority.
Lived experience is a legitimate and essential source of quality evidence.
People with serious mental illness have significantly higher physical health risks that nurses must actively address.
Examine who benefits — and who remains excluded
Equity analysis is not optional. It is a professional and ethical responsibility.
Next: Continue with GNPS Programme 8 — Section 4 for further clinical application and NCLEX preparation practice.

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 8 · Level 3 — Compassionate Mental Health Care

bullets.label: SECTION 4: DIGITAL MENTAL HEALTH & GLOBAL COLLABORATION

cards.title: Why Digital Mental Health Matters
cards.body: Digital platforms, telehealth, apps and predictive tools can significantly expand access to mental health support. However, they also introduce risks: privacy breaches, digital exclusion, misinformation and over-reliance on algorithms.

bullets.label: Global nursing professionals use technology critically and ethically — balancing innovation with safeguarding.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing Section 4, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Critically assess digital mental health tools for evidence, safety and suitability.
Safeguard therapeutic relationships and patient confidentiality in digital settings.
Identify digital exclusion and algorithmic bias affecting vulnerable populations.
Contribute to global mental health learning with cultural sensitivity.

cards.title: Core Concept: Tele-Mental Health
cards.body: Opportunities & Responsibilities

bullets.label: Virtual care can dramatically improve access
bullets.text: Virtual care can dramatically improve access for patients in remote or underserved areas. However, nurses delivering tele-mental health must address key clinical duties:

bullets.label: Confirm patient identity at every session
Establish and document emergency escalation plans
Maintain robust privacy and data security
Recognise what cannot be safely assessed remotely

cards.title: Apps & Online Support Tools
cards.body: Evidence-Informed

bullets.label: Only recommend tools with a clear evidence base and transparent development methodology.
Digital tools should complement, not replace, professional clinical assessment and support.
Apps must never substitute urgent mental health assessment — always have crisis pathways in place.

cards.title: Data, Algorithms & Professional Judgement
cards.body: Predictive Tools: Opportunity & Risk

bullets.label: Algorithms can support clinical decision-making
bullets.text: Algorithms can support clinical decision-making by identifying patterns in large datasets. But data reflects the populations it was gathered from — biases can lead to unequal outcomes.

bullets.label: Explain limitations clearly to patients and teams

cards.title: Global Mental Health Collaboration
cards.body: Effective global collaboration means more than sharing knowledge — it requires respecting local resources, cultural frameworks and community expertise.

bullets.label: Design services that reach all communities regardless of geography or income.
Adapt global frameworks to local beliefs, languages and healing traditions.
Support systems that communities can maintain with their own resources long-term.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Rural Video Reviews
cards.body: What Good Practice Looks Like

bullets.label: A rural mental health service introduces
bullets.text: A rural mental health service introduces video-based reviews to reduce travel barriers. Leaders proactively address potential risks by establishing:

bullets.label: Privacy guidance for all video sessions
Crisis escalation pathways for remote emergencies
Telephone alternatives for patients without internet access
Technology improves access — without becoming the only route to care.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Technology Supports, Not Replaces

bullets.label: Therapeutic judgement and human connection remain at the core of mental health nursing.
Every remote care arrangement must have a documented crisis escalation pathway before it begins.
Ensure digital tools are safe, confidential and accessible to all patients — not just the digitally connected.
Translate international best practice into culturally and contextually appropriate care.

cards.title: Programme 8 Complete — Well Done!
cards.body: By completing GNPS Programme 8 · Level 3, you have developed the advanced perspective of a Global Nursing Professional — ready to:

bullets.label: Champion person-centred, recovery-focused care across all settings.
Apply least-restrictive principles and advocate for patient dignity.
Use technology ethically to expand equitable mental health access.
Promote mental wellbeing for all populations, locally and globally.
